findings: Decode is not attention-bound. gemma4_attention_decode_class_kernel is 50.04 ms, 1.6% of the 3067.9 ms total, so the 2X decode target has to come out of the expert matmuls and the activation packing, which together are about 71%.

The single largest line is the Q4_K MoE gate/up at 860.49 ms, 28.0%, in 1827 calls - 28.5 per decode step, one per layer. The Q5_1 expert down is next at 530.48 ms, 17.3%, also 1827 calls, and it runs a selected-GEMV kernel as expected for decode.

Activation packing is the surprise: gguf_k_pack8_prefill_out_kernel appears twice, at 576.92 ms in 12915 calls and 222.23 ms in 64 calls, together 26.0% of decode. The 12915 is 202 launches per decode step, which at 44.7 us per launch means decode is spending a quarter of its time in a large number of very small packing launches. Reducing the launch count is therefore a candidate lever in its own right, separate from making any single kernel faster.

The 'prefill' in those kernel names is historical, not a routing error. gemma4_moe_prefill_route_enabled requires lanes >= _PREFILL_MIN_LANES_PER_EXPERT * num_experts, and decode has lanes = 1 * top_k = 8 against 128 experts, so the row-reusing prefill route is correctly off and the selected/GEMV family is what runs. I checked this because 54% of decode time sits in kernels named prefill, and the names alone would have read as a mis-dispatch.

The 202-per-step packing launch count is now explained. The kernel lives in gguf_q8_0_pack8_gemv.py, whose docstring calls it 'the decode-shaped' kernel, so it is the q8_0 dense decode GEMV and the 'prefill' in its name is historical. 12915 calls over 64 steps and 29 layers is 7 per layer, which is the seven dense projections - q, k, v, o, gate, up, down. Each is a separate launch because each has its own weight matrix, so this is not a batching oversight; the lever is the per-launch cost and the kernel's own efficiency at the decode shape, not a reduction in launch count by combining unrelated projections.

The Q4_K MoE gate/up, the largest decode line at 28.0%, is memory-bound at 38.5 GB/s - about 15% of the 8060S's roughly 250 GB/s. Arithmetic: q4_k gate_up is 128 experts x 2816 x 1408 at 4.5 bpw = 285 MB total, top-8 routing reads 17.8 MB per token, and across 29 layers that is 517.4 MB in 13.45 ms. So the kernel is not compute-limited; there is roughly a 4-6x bandwidth headroom on this line alone, which is more than the whole 2X decode target.

A pre-packed decode GEMV for this exact path already exists and is not wired. hipengine_gguf_q4_k_selected_pack8_gemv_bf16_bf16_out is defined at gguf_q4_k_gemv.py:47 with a wrapper at :1503, and a repository-wide grep finds no caller outside its own module. The q5_k and q6_k equivalents in gguf_k_selected_pack8_gemv.py do have wiring. Whether the q4_k pack8 path was never finished or was retired is not yet established, so the next unit is to find out why it is unwired before assuming it is the answer - pack8 needs a weight repack at load time, so it is not free.

Third instance of a historical 'prefill' in a kernel name, recorded so the pattern stops costing time. gguf_q4_k_selected_prefill_out_kernel is defined in gguf_q4_k_gemv.hip, so it is the decode GEMV, and gemma4_project_experts_rows reports its route as selected_gemv at decode. The route is correct. I checked this because the profile appeared to show a prefill kernel running during decode, and the check cost one grep while the wrong conclusion would have cost a unit.

The unwired q4_k pack8 GEMV is never-finished, not retired, and the mechanism is now identified. Evidence: the symbol was introduced by 7371f7c0b, a Qwen35 decode commit; the device kernel (launch_gguf_q4_k_selected_pack8_gemv_out, gguf_q4_k_gemv.hip:1432) and its extern C entry (:2894) both exist; tests/test_gpu_gguf_expert_pack8_gemv.py covers the family; and a repository-wide grep finds no caller for the q4_k wrapper anywhere, including in qwen35_gguf_runner.py, which does call the q5_k and q6_k pack8 wrappers at :38900. The registry variant map in gguf_k_gemv.py registers selected_pack8_gemv for q8_0 (:1599), q5_k (:1641) and q6_k (:1679) but not q4_k. gemma4_project_experts_selected resolves its kernel through that registry by (backend, linear, quant_key, variant), so an unregistered variant is unreachable by construction rather than by choice. This is the concrete instance of the objective's premise that Qwen35 work transfers: the same family is wired for three quant types and missing for the one Gemma 4 uses for its expert gate/up.

The pack8 layout for q4_k already exists, so wiring the selected pack8 GEMV is a small, well-scoped change rather than a new repack pass. hipengine/quant/gguf_q4_k.py:147 documents a 'Lossless pack8 layout for GGUF Q4_K GEMV' and imports Q4_K_PACK8_SHAPE from hipengine.quant.gguf_repack. What is missing is only the plumbing: q8_0 (gguf_k_gemv.py:518), q5_k (:613) and q6_k (:689) each build their selected pack8 wrapper with _make_selected_pack8_wrapper and each have a selected_pack8_gemv_bf16_bf16_out entry in the variant map (:1599, :1641, :1679), while q4_k's wrapper at gguf_q4_k_gemv.py:1503 uses _make_selected_wrapper instead and has no map entry. There is also an existing switch for this family: HIPENGINE_GGUF_GEMV_DECODE, described in gguf_linear.py:161-165 as the opt-in for the GGUF pack8 GEMV decode family (P9.B), selecting the pack8_gemv_decode_* kernels over the legacy pack8_gemv_* decoders. So q4_k selected appears to be the one quant type the P9.B1-P9.B4b work did not reach, and the named clearing step is: build the q4_k selected pack8 wrapper, add the variant-map entry, and confirm the weight carries the pack8 layout at load.

The thread resolves: the pack8 expert GEMV for q4_k is already written, tested and registered, and the reason gemma4 does not use it is a registry layer mismatch. gguf_expert_pack8_gemv.py registers gguf_q4_k_expert_pack8_selected_bf16_bf16_out under KernelKey('hip_gfx1100', 'moe_linear', 'gguf_q4_k', 'expert_pack8_selected_bf16_bf16_out') at :145, with q5_k and q6_k alongside at :150 and :154, and register_gguf_expert_pack8_gemv_kernels() is invoked at module import (:263) so the entry is live. tests/test_gpu_gguf_expert_pack8_gemv.py covers the family, and repack_gguf_q4_k_pack8 (gguf_q4_k.py:1316) produces the GGUFQ4KPack8 layout it needs. Meanwhile gemma4_project_experts_selected resolves with KernelKey(weight.backend, 'linear', quant_key, _SELECTED_VARIANT) - layer 'linear', variant 'selected_gemv' - and a repository-wide grep for expert_pack8 finds nothing under hipengine/kernels/hip_gfx1100/gemma4/ at all. So the expert pack8 route exists for this quant type and this backend, is registered under the moe_linear layer, and the gemma4 MoE path never looks there. The named clearing step is to have the MoE route resolve moe_linear / expert_pack8_selected first and fall back to the current linear / selected_gemv route, which is the fallback the existing dispatch already provides for a missing kernel.

The fix is two parts, and the order matters. Layout materialization is declaration-driven: hipengine/loading/qwen35_gguf_materialize.py:147 maps LAYOUT_Q4_K_PACK8 to _ResidentRepack(Q4_K_PACK8_SHAPE, repack_gguf_q4_k_pack8), and laguna does the same at laguna_gguf_materialize.py:1022, so a weight carries the pack8 layout only if its loader declares that layout. Qwen35's MoE then resolves an explicit KernelKey map at qwen35_gguf_runner.py:35458 mapping gguf_q4_k/q5_k/q6_k to the moe_linear / expert_pack8_selected_bf16_bf16_out variants. Gemma 4 has neither half: no pack8 mention in its loader, and a MoE route that resolves linear / selected_gemv. So part one is to declare the q4_k pack8 layout in Gemma 4's materialization and part two is to resolve the moe_linear key, with part one first - a lookup change alone would hand the kernel an unpacked weight, which reads garbage rather than failing, so the layout declaration is the safety property and not an optimization. This ordering is the reason the earlier plan was sequenced that way, and it is now confirmed from the materializer rather than assumed.

Correction to the size of the next unit: Gemma 4's materializer has no resident-repack machinery at all. grep for _RESIDENT_REPACKS, LAYOUT_ constants and repack in hipengine/loading/gemma4_gguf_materialize.py returns nothing, while qwen35_gguf_materialize.py carries a full _RESIDENT_REPACKS mapping (LAYOUT_Q4_K_PACK8 through the q5_k/q6_k/q8_0 entries) and laguna_gguf_materialize.py defines its own LAYOUT_Q4_K_PACK8. So part one of the fix is not a declaration line to add - it is porting resident-repack materialization to Gemma 4's loader, or producing the pack8 layout for its expert tensors by another route. The previous entry described part one as 'declare the q4_k pack8 layout', which understated it, and this corrects the estimate rather than leaving it to be discovered mid-implementation. The ordering argument is unaffected: the weight must carry the layout before any route change can be correct.

The next unit is a port, not new architecture, and Gemma 4's own loader says so. hipengine/loading/gemma4_gguf_device.py:15 states 'No repack step. launch_gguf_linear serves the raw layout for every quant ... so resident-layout conversion is a later performance question', and the module defines exactly two layouts, LAYOUT_RAW_GGUF (:44) and LAYOUT_DENSE_F32 (:45), with a dispatch in materialize_gemma4_gguf_device_weight (:203) that branches on spec.layout (:215, :225) and raises on anything else (:228). So a resident-layout step can be inserted where that dispatch is, which makes part one a port of the qwen35 _RESIDENT_REPACKS pattern rather than a new materialization path. The module's own comment calls resident-layout conversion a later performance question; this profile is that question answered, with roughly 4-6x of bandwidth headroom on a line that is 28.0% of decode. Note also that gemma4_gguf_materialize.py is the CPU reference materializer (Gemma4GGUFReferenceWeights, importing kernels.cpu_reference.gemma4), not the device path, so the earlier grep for repack machinery there was looking in the wrong file.
limits: One prompt length, one output length, one box, one profiling run. Decode cost varies with context length - the earlier length curve showed decode falling from 21.91 to 19.57 tok/s between 128 and 2048 prompt tokens - so this profile describes a 128-token context.
